title: New lower bounds for CDS and $f$-routing
abstract: Understanding the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is relevant to complexity theory, cryptography, quantum gravity, and related areas. A central special case is $f$-routing, motivated in part by quantum position verification. Proving lower bounds on its entanglement cost in the fully robust setting has been a major open problem in NLQC.   Motivated by this problem, we establish two related lower bounds. First, we study the shared-randomness cost of robust conditional disclosure of secrets (CDS). The connection between CDS and $f$-routing established by Allerstorfer et al. (Quantum 2024) makes understanding the randomness complexity of robust CDS a natural step toward lower bounds for the fully robust routing problem. We show that the shared-randomness cost of robust CDS is lower bounded by the logarithm of deterministic SMP communication complexity, even when communication and private randomness are unrestricted. Our lower bound is tight for the equality function.   Second, we consider one-sided-perfect $f$-routing, in which the protocol is exact on one input class and has constant error on the other. By exploiting the positivity of the low-rank matrix arising in the method of Asadi, Culf, and May (ITCS 2025), we derive a general lower bound on the entanglement cost in terms of sign rank. In particular, this yields a linear lower bound on the entanglement cost of routing for the inner-product function in both one-sided-perfect settings, matching the known upper bound.
summary: This paper derives strong lower bounds for the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation tasks, particularly $f$-routing, and for the shared randomness required in Conditional Disclosure of Secrets (CDS). By connecting these two problems, the authors establish bounds based on the sign rank of associated Boolean matrices, advancing the understanding of quantum information complexity.
main_problem: The paper establishes lower bounds on the entanglement cost for Non-Local Quantum Computation (NLQC) tasks, specifically focusing on $f$-routing and Conditional Disclosure of Secrets (CDS).
main_result: They derive a general lower bound for one-sided-perfect $f$-routing based on the sign rank of the associated matrix, and establish a shared-randomness lower bound for robust CDS.
method: The authors utilize techniques involving the sign rank of Boolean matrices and establish connections between the randomness complexity of CDS and the entanglement cost of $f$-routing.
model_or_system: The study analyzes abstract quantum information tasks: $f$-routing (a non-local computation task) and CDS (a secure multi-party computation primitive). These tasks are modeled using quantum communication protocols involving shared entangled states.
key_observables: Entanglement cost ($\log d_E$), Shared-randomness cost ($\log q$), Sign rank ($	ext{signrank}(S_f)$), and Deterministic SMP communication complexity ($D_{\parallel}(f)$).
important_parameters: The bounds are derived for one-sided-perfect protocols, and the results are shown to be tight for specific functions like the equality function.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the connection between CDS and $f$-routing, and the use of the sign-rank method, which is most directly applicable to one-sided-perfect settings.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the setup for local vs. non-local quantum computation. Figure 2 illustrates the setup for the Conditional Disclosure of Secrets (CDS) task.
paper_structure: The paper first addresses the robust CDS lower bound using shared randomness, connecting it to deterministic communication complexity. It then tackles one-sided-perfect $f$-routing by exploiting the positivity of the low-rank matrix, yielding a bound in terms of sign rank, and finally relates these bounds across different complexity measures.
why_interesting: The work provides rigorous, information-theoretic lower bounds for fundamental quantum tasks, which can guide the design of quantum protocols and test the limits of quantum communication complexity.
